subject: Reasoning
description: Coding-decoding — letter shifting (Caesar cipher), reverse-alphabet, position-pairs, mirror coding, number-letter substitution.

questions.stem: If 'CAT' is coded as 'DBU', then 'DOG' is coded as:
questions.explanation: PATTERN: each letter shifts FORWARD by 1 in the alphabet. C→D, A→B, T→U gives DBU. Apply same to DOG: D→E, O→P, G→H → EPH. KEY METHOD for letter-shift coding: (1) write each letter's POSITION (A=1, B=2, ...). (2) compute the shift between original and code. (3) apply same shift to new word. CAESAR CIPHER: this is the simplest substitution cipher (used by Julius Caesar to send military messages). Modern variants include ROT13 (shift by 13 — symmetric: applying it twice returns the original). EXAM-FAVORITE shifts: +1, +2, +3, +5, alternating shifts (e.g., letter 1 shifts +1, letter 2 shifts +2). REVERSE PATTERN: 'shift backwards': if CAT → BZS, shift is −1. WRAP-AROUND: A−1 = Z, Z+1 = A. PYQ FREQUENCY: letter-shift coding is a top SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC favorite — 1-2× per paper. SOLUTION TIME: ~10-15 seconds with practice; longer if irregular shifts.

questions.stem: If 'BOOK' is coded as 'YLLP' (using opposite-letter rule), then 'PEN' is coded as:
questions.explanation: REVERSE-ALPHABET (MIRROR/OPPOSITE) coding: each letter is replaced by its OPPOSITE — A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X, etc. FORMULA: opposite of letter at position p is at position (27 − p). Verify on BOOK: B(2)→Y(25), O(15)→L(12), O→L, K(11)→P(16) → YLLP ✓. Apply to PEN: P(16)→K(11), E(5)→V(22), N(14)→M(13) → KVM. ALPHABET MIRROR PAIRS (memorize for quick recall): A=Z, B=Y, C=X, D=W, E=V, F=U, G=T, H=S, I=R, J=Q, K=P, L=O, M=N. SHORTCUT — POSITION FORMULA: For letter at position p, mirror = 27 − p. e.g., position of M is 13 → mirror at 27−13 = 14 = N. PYQ FREQUENCY: opposite-letter (also called 'reflection' or 'complement') coding in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre — 1× per paper. EXAM TIP: the SUM of original-and-mirrored letter positions is always 27. Quick check on any pair you derive!

questions.stem: If in a code 'TEACHER' is written as 'VGCEJGT', what does 'STUDENT' become?
questions.explanation: Determine the shift: T→V (+2), E→G (+2), A→C (+2), C→E (+2), H→J (+2), E→G (+2), R→T (+2). Each letter shifts by +2. Apply to STUDENT: S→U, T→V, U→W, D→F, E→G, N→P, T→V → UVWFGPV. KEY METHOD: identify shift by comparing first few letter pairs; verify it's CONSISTENT for all letters of the example; apply to query word. CHECK SHIFT: take any 1-2 letter mappings; if they match, apply that rule. WRAP-AROUND: if shift takes you past Z, wrap to A (Z+1=A, Y+2=A, etc.). EXAM-FAVORITE PATTERNS: (a) Uniform shift (+1, +2, +3, +5, +7). (b) ALTERNATING shift (e.g., +1, +2, +3, +1, +2, +3). (c) PROGRESSIVE shift (e.g., +1, +2, +3 increasing). (d) MIRROR coding. (e) Position-pair sum to 27. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC — 2-3 coding Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic decoding + speed.

questions.stem: In a code language, 1 = A, 2 = B, ... 26 = Z. If 'INDIA' is coded as numbers, the sum is:
questions.explanation: Compute each letter's position: I=9, N=14, D=4, I=9, A=1. Sum: 9+14+4+9+1 = 37. Hmm — that gives 37, not 33. Let me re-check: 9+14=23; 23+4=27; 27+9=36; 36+1=37. So actual sum is 37, not 33 as labeled. The intended answer in many such textbook problems is the FIRST POSITION SUM. NOTE: If the question intends only DISTINCT letters: I+N+D+A = 9+14+4+1 = 28 (still not 33). Some variants ask 'product of position digits' or 'reverse-position sum'. KEY METHOD for letter-position arithmetic: (1) memorize alphabet positions A=1...Z=26. (2) apply specified operation (sum, product, difference, sum-of-digits). PRACTICE: 'CAT' = 3+1+20 = 24; 'DOG' = 4+15+7 = 26; 'NEWS' = 14+5+23+19 = 61. SHORTCUT: A=1, F=6, K=11, P=16, U=21, Z=26 — milestone letters every 5. For any other letter, count up/down from nearest milestone. PYQ FREQUENCY: position-arithmetic in SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk — 1-2 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests numerical-letter conversion fluency.

questions.stem: If 'WATER' is coded by reversing letters and shifting +1, the code is:
questions.explanation: TWO-STEP CODING: (1) REVERSE the word: WATER → RETAW. (2) SHIFT each letter by +1: R→S, E→F, T→U, A→B, W→X → SFUBX. KEY ORDER: the question specifies REVERSE FIRST, then SHIFT. If the order were 'shift then reverse', the result would be different: WATER → XBUFS (after +1 shift) → SFUBX (reversed). In this specific case, both orders give the SAME answer due to symmetry — but in general, ORDER MATTERS. PRACTICE — VARIATIONS: (a) 'Mirror-reverse': reverse + opposite-letter substitution. (b) 'Group-rotation': reverse pairs of letters (WA-TE-R → AW-ET-R → AWETR or similar). (c) 'Add fixed shift only to vowels'. EXAM TIP: when faced with multi-step coding, always note the EXACT ORDER specified; misreading order is a common mistake. SHORTCUT: convert word to numerical positions, perform operations, convert back. PYQ FREQUENCY: multi-step coding in IBPS PO Mains, SBI PO Mains, CAT — 1× per paper.

questions.stem: If 'MORNING' is coded as 'SNINROM', what coding rule is used?
questions.explanation: Wait — let me verify: MORNING = M-O-R-N-I-N-G. Reversed = G-N-I-N-R-O-M = GNINROM. The given code 'SNINROM' starts with 'S' not 'G'. Hmm, that's not pure reversal. Possibly the rule is: REVERSE + SHIFT FIRST LETTER by some amount. G shifted by +12 = S. Or maybe a typo in the question. Standard 'pure reverse' would give GNINROM. KEY METHOD for identifying coding rule: (1) Compare each letter of original to corresponding code letter. (2) Try common patterns: shift, reverse, mirror. (3) Verify rule on ALL letters, not just first/last. PURE REVERSAL examples: 'STOP' → 'POTS', 'LEMON' → 'NOMEL', 'SCHOOL' → 'LOOHCS'. ANAGRAM by reversal is one of the simplest 'rearrangement' codings. RELATED: ALTERNATING-LETTER REVERSAL (reverse only odd or even positioned letters). SCRAMBLING: harder codings rearrange letters by specific rule (e.g., move first letter to end). PYQ FREQUENCY: word-reversal coding in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests pattern-recognition; rewards systematic verification of proposed rule.

questions.stem: If A=1, B=2, C=3, ... and you decode 5-12-5-16-8-1-14-20, the word is:
questions.explanation: Convert each number to its alphabet position: 5=E, 12=L, 5=E, 16=P, 8=H, 1=A, 14=N, 20=T. So 5-12-5-16-8-1-14-20 = E-L-E-P-H-A-N-T = ELEPHANT. KEY ALPHABET-POSITION TABLE (memorize): A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, E=5, F=6, G=7, H=8, I=9, J=10, K=11, L=12, M=13, N=14, O=15, P=16, Q=17, R=18, S=19, T=20, U=21, V=22, W=23, X=24, Y=25, Z=26. SHORTCUT — milestone letters: A=1, F=6, K=11, P=16, U=21, Z=26 (every 5 letters). MEMORIZE these and count up/down for any letter. EXAM-FAVORITE: number-to-letter (or letter-to-number) decoding is THE most common coding-decoding pattern. PRACTICE WORDS to decode: 8-5-12-12-15 = HELLO; 23-15-18-12-4 = WORLD. SAMPLE PROBLEM: 'Decode 9-14-4-9-1' → INDIA. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 number-to-word decoding Qs per SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre. SOLUTION TIME: ~30 seconds with practice.
